info.title: Power Pages Sitewide API
info.description:
The Power Pages **sitewide** API -- the control plane the Power Pages maker portal calls to manage sites rather than to build them. It lists a tenant's sites, reads and writes their app settings, drives the go-live and site-health checks, and configures the Azure Front Door WAF, the DDoS diagnostic setting and the security agent that sit in front of a published site.

It is **not** the surface a site is authored on. Site content lives in Dataverse tables and is reached through the Dataverse Web API (spec:dataverse); this host is the provisioning and governance plane above that, and the two share no route.

It is also **not** the `/powerpages/` family on the Power Platform API host, which spec:ppapi documents over 27 paths. That family is a namespace of PPAPI, reached on the global and tenant hosts and versioned with an `api-version` like the rest of PPAPI. This spec is a separate service on a separate host with its own `/api/v1/` prefix and no versioning at all. Two Power Pages control surfaces exist; a reader arriving from a capture needs to know which host they saw.

**No operation here takes an `api-version`** -- not as a query parameter, not as a header, not as a path segment beyond the literal `/api/v1` prefix. All 39 call sites read from the shipped client send the bare route, and the three routes observed on the wire sent none either. This is a finding, not an omission: do not add one.

**There is also no hostname in the client.** Every call is written against the literal `https://portals-provision/...` and the host is substituted at request time from a per-cloud settings key. See `info.x-cloud-hosts`.

Unofficial and reverse-engineered -- see the [README](https://github.com/AdamCoulterOz/powerplatform-apis/tree/main/powerpages) for how it was derived and which parts are verified.

x-cloud-hosts.description: appSettings ring key -> the value of `powerPortalSitewideApiHostname` for that ring. This is a per-cloud lookup inside the client's own settings, not a hostname anyone assembles per request, and no endpoint publishes it -- which is why it is written out in full here as well as in `servers`.

notes.default: The fallback when no ring matches. Quoted verbatim from the settings object.
notes.tie: The TIP ring. **Inferred.** The extract's prose names a `tip` ring served by `portalsitewide-tip`, while the ring key vocabulary it publishes elsewhere spells the key `tie`. The host is certain; that this key carries it is a reading of two facts that do not quite meet.
notes.test: **The one host that breaks the pattern**: the prefix is `sitewide-test`, not `portalsitewide-test`. Anyone templating `portalsitewide-{ring}` will get this one wrong.
notes.preview: Shares the production host. Quoted verbatim from the settings object.
notes.prod: Commercial production. Quoted verbatim from the settings object.
notes.gov: US Government Community Cloud -- still on `.dynamics.com`, unlike the other sovereign rings.
notes.high: US Government GCC High. Different domain: `.portal-infra.microsoftdynamics.us`.
notes.dod: US Department of Defense. No ring suffix on the label at all.
notes.mooncake: China, operated by 21Vianet. No ring suffix.

verification.note: **None of these hosts has been reached from here.** The three `live` operations were observed on this API on 2026-09-05, but the capture that witnessed them recorded status codes only and did not record which host served them, so no entry in this table carries a reachability claim. The table is the client's settings object, transcribed.

x-source-builds.description: The artefacts every `ppac-spa` claim in this spec rests on.
x-source-builds.sourceMaps: None. The sourcemap host is decommissioned, so every claim graded `ppac-spa` here was read out of minified JavaScript.

x-verb-unknown.description: Routes on this host that are real but have **no established HTTP verb**, and are therefore deliberately absent from `paths`. In both cases the URL is assembled into a local variable and the evidence window closes before the call that consumes it, so the verb is not recoverable from what was mined. Guessing one would put a wrong method in a spec that reads as though it had been observed.

routes.known: The write half of `setup_getInstancePackages`. Six query parameters are visible, the last (`orgUrl`) truncated mid-token. Headers: `Prefer`, plus `x-ms-environment-id` when the environment is known. Its telemetry scope falls back to the literal `sitewide-api`, which is the only place the client names this service in words.

The URL is bound to a module-level constant next to a generic query-string builder that drops null and empty values and URL-encodes the rest. No parameter name and no verb survive in the evidence, so nothing but the path is known.

x-notes.note:
**The client contains no hostname for this service.** Every call is written against the literal `https://portals-provision/...`, and the shell's HTTP client looks `portals-provision` up in a service registry (map key `swprovision`), takes the endpoint for the current cloud from the settings key `powerPortalSitewideApiHostname`, attaches that service's token, and rewrites the hostname before the request leaves.

Two things follow. A reader of these bundles who takes the URL literally will attribute all forty routes to a host called `portals-provision`, which does not exist. And because the endpoint is a settings lookup rather than an assembly, there is no discovery call a client can make -- the table in `info.x-cloud-hosts` is the whole of it.

**Nothing on this API carries an `api-version`.** Every other Power Platform surface in this corpus versions its requests; this one does not, on any of the 39 mined call sites or on the three routes seen live. The version is in the path (`/api/v1`) and nowhere else. A client that adds `?api-version=...` out of habit is sending a parameter this spec has no evidence the service reads.

**How the methods here were established, and where that stops.** The extract binds a verb only when the URL is passed directly to the call that carries it; 23 of the 39 records arrived that way. Fourteen more are bound in this spec, by reading the verb off the same statement in the evidence string: the URL is assigned to a local (`var l = "https://portals-provision/..."`) and consumed two tokens later by `client.get(l, ...)` or `client.post(l, ...)` in the same visible window. That is the same call site, just spread over two statements, and it is the same client object the bound records use.

Two records could not be bound and are **not** in `paths`. They are listed in `info.x-verb-unknown` with what is known about them. No verb anywhere in this spec is a guess.

**Five POSTs send a header object as their request body.** `RunDiagnostic`, `UpdateLicenseCheckInfo`, `UpdateSiteHealthCheckInfo`, `UpdateSiteVisibility` and `UpdatePortalName` all call `post(url, {Prefer: 'odata.include-annotations="*"'})`, and the second positional argument of that client is the body rather than the config. So each sends that object as JSON and sets no `Prefer` header. `RunDiagnostic` sends the enclosing `{headers: {...}}` wrapper as well.

Every one of these operations carries the misplacement in its `requestBody` because that is what goes on the wire. None of them is evidence that the service wants a body.

**Several routes return JSON that has been serialised twice.** The client calls `JSON.parse()` on an already-parsed response body on `InstallFlow`, on the generic `powerPortal` POST and on `GetPortalAppSetting`, and the extract carries the same observation as a note on `listPortalsByOrgId`. `GetPortalAppSetting` goes further and lower-cases the string first, which is only necessary for `True`/`False` -- a .NET boolean rendered as text and repaired on the client.

None of this is a response schema: no reply from any of these routes has been seen here. It is the shape the client's own code implies, which is a weaker claim, and it is recorded as prose in each operation's `200` description rather than as a schema for exactly that reason. This spec declares no response schemas at all.

**The route names are not normalised, and two of them read as mistakes.** `createDDOSDaignosticSetting`, `deleteDDOSDaignosticSetting` and `isDDOSDaignosticSettingEnabled` transpose `Diagnostic`; the governance route drops to lower-case `powerportal` where every other route on the host uses `powerPortal`. Both are reproduced verbatim -- correcting either would produce a path that does not exist.

**Two routes take their last path segment from the caller.** The client builds `/api/v1/powerPortal/{apiName}` and `/api/v1/powerPortal/SearchSummary/{apiName}` from an argument, so these are route *families* rather than routes, and every concrete `/api/v1/powerPortal/...` operation in this spec is also reachable through the first of them. No literal `apiName` value appears in the mined chunks: the helpers are generic and their callers were not in the chunk set.

The live `ListPortals` route has exactly that shape. That is a resemblance worth noticing and not a corroboration, which is why it carries no `x-corroborated-by`.

**Three operations are graded `live` and none of them appears in the bundles.** `ListPortals`, `ZAP/GetDeepScanEnabledPortalByTenant` and `dlp/policies/portals/disableAnonymousAccessInPowerPages/status` were observed on the wire on 2026-09-05. Searching the whole extract for `ListPortals`, `ZAP`, `GetDeepScanEnabled` and `disableAnonymousAccess` returns nothing, so no bundle route was merged into them: the nearest neighbours -- `listPortalsByOrgId` and `dlp/policyErrorSetting` -- differ in more than casing and are kept as separate routes.

The capture recorded status codes only. So these three carry `x-probe-verified` for the route and the method, and their `200` descriptions assert nothing about a body, because no body was kept.

**A bundle shows what a client can send, not what a service accepted.** Every parameter, body field and route graded `ppac-spa` here is one the shipped code is capable of producing, including on branches no session reached. That makes the coverage wider than a capture and the confirmation weaker, and it is why 37 of the 40 operations carry no `x-probe-verified`.

One consequence worth stating: the extract's own `requestBodyFields` list is unreliable on this host -- it collects destructured argument names and fallback-object keys as though they were body fields. Request bodies in this spec were re-read from the evidence strings instead, which is why most of them are empty objects.

**The audience for this host is not documented here because it is not known.** The shell attaches whatever token its service registry holds for `swprovision`, and the registry entry's resource id is not in the mined chunks. Every other spec in this corpus names a scope; this one deliberately declares no `security` rather than guess one from the hostname, which is the mistake spec:athena records as having been made against a differently-named service.

servers.description: Commercial and GCC rings. Pick `hostPrefix` by resolving the client's ring through `info.x-cloud-hosts`. The other five clouds are separate entries below because their domains differ.

hostPrefix.description: The host label for the ring. **Not a uniform pattern**: the test ring is `sitewide-test`, dropping the `portal` the other three carry, so `portalsitewide-{ring}` is wrong for one of the four. `portalsitewide-nam` serves both `prod` and `preview`; `portalsitewide-tip` serves `default`, `preprod` and the TIP ring.

x-notes.note: **A config object, not just a header, ends up in the body here.** The call is `post(url, {headers: {Prefer: ...}})`, so the whole axios config -- `headers` wrapper included -- is serialised as the request body and no `Prefer` header is sent.
